problem.claim: How to incorporate human expertise into algorithmic prediction by using human judgment on inputs that algorithms cannot distinguish.

gap.claim: Predictive algorithms may lack information used by experts because it is not encoded in their training data; the framework addresses this human-AI collaboration challenge.

contributions.claim: Introduces a framework that selectively incorporates human feedback using algorithmic indistinguishability.
Shows that the method provably improves any feasible algorithmic predictor and quantifies the improvement.
Demonstrates instance-level human complementarity in an X-ray classification task, where the identifiable subset is nearly 30% of patients.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe their framework for incorporating human expertise into algorithmic predictions as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report a provable performance improvement for any feasible algorithmic predictor, with the improvement precisely quantified.
The authors report that algorithms often outperform humans on average, while human judgment improves predictions on specific instances identifiable ex ante.
In an X-ray classification task, the authors report that this subset comprises nearly 30% of the patient population.

narrative_sequence.summary: Introduces a framework for incorporating human expertise into prediction.
Defines algorithmic indistinguishability as inputs that look the same to predictive algorithms, then links expert judgments to unencoded information.
Uses indistinguishability to test for side information and selectively incorporate feedback, with a claimed provable improvement.
Reports average algorithmic superiority alongside instance-specific human gains, including a nearly 30% X-ray-task subset.
Positions heterogeneity discovery as a way to enable human-AI collaboration.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns a diagnostic test for expert side information with a selective feedback mechanism, and then reports both theoretical and task-specific evidence.

lessons.interpretation: A strong learning-card pattern is to connect the proposed construct, operational test, intervention, and evidence in one chain.
lessons.application: For a new human-AI prediction method, define the disagreement or indistinguishability condition, explain how it triggers human input, and report theory and instance-level evaluation separately.
lessons.exception: This structure is unsuitable when the work has no operational criterion for selecting cases or no evidence beyond a proposal.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the predictor class or meaning of “feasible,” nor the formula or magnitude of the quantified improvement.
It does not describe how the ex-ante identifiable subset is detected, the X-ray dataset or protocol, or the comparison details.
